newsitem.title: USA: Hinsdale Health Sys. debt affirmed at BBB by S&P.
newsitem.headline: Hinsdale Health Sys. debt affirmed at BBB by S&P.

text.p: NEW YORK, Oct 15 - Standard & Poor's Corp today has affirmed its triple-B' rating on Illinois Health Facilities Authority's bonds, issued for Hinsdale Health System as follows:
-- $53.7 million revenue refunding bonds series 1993A and 1993B,
-- $77.4 million revenue refunding bonds series 1990A-1990E, and
-- $5.3 million revenue and refunding bonds series 1990F, issued by Wisconsin Health & Education Facilities Authority.

The rating is based on good financial performance and balance sheet, good debt service coverage, and stable market position. In the first three years (1990-1992) since Hinsdale Health System's four obligated group members spun off from the Adventist Health System, financial performance improved dramatically.

However, since 1993, financial performance declined modestly, but is still strong. Obligated group excess margins for 1994 were 5.2% ($11.3 million) and 4.2% ($9.1 million) in 1995. Lower results in 1995 were expected. Increasing pressure on revenue has resulted in flat total revenues since 1992, with a small declining trend since 1994. Maximum annual debt service coverage was good in 1995 at 2.3 times (x). The balance sheet in 1995 is strong with 105 days' cash on hand, stable since 1992. Debt to capitalization has declined modestly to 59.5% in 1995 from 69.2% back in 1991.

The 344 bed (was 417 staffed beds in 1994) continues to anchor the system, accounting for 80.3% of the obligated group's total revenues (from 73% in 1990), and all excess income. The 115 bed GlenOaks Medical Center has had negative excess income in four of the last five years. Both facilities have stable market positions. Major mergers or affiliations in this market are inevitable as Chicago's regional networks are expanding.

The outlook is based on expectations that continued revenue declines will be managed through continued reductions of operating costs. Competition, lack of system diversity, continued losses at GlenOaks, and other external forces such as managed care will continue to pressure the system, Standard & Poor's said.
